```{r library}
library(orchestraManifest)
```

## Why

A package author who has just built a new estimator and wants its result
readable by every other member of the orchestra asks a narrow, practical
question: *if I hand my result to another package as an*
`orchestra_manifest`*, what exactly am I promising it, and how does it find
out the moment I break that promise?* This vignette answers both halves --
what the promise is, and what happens when it is broken, through a
corrupted payload, an unrecognised schema version, or a derived result that
has lost track of what it was derived from.

A collection of analytics components becomes a framework only when one
component's output is another's input by construction. The alternative is
what most multi-package stacks actually do -- each component returns its own
list or data frame, and every pairing needs a bespoke adapter written by
whoever wired it, checked by nobody, and silently wrong the day either side
changes shape.

## What

The manifest is the single result type that removes those adapters. An
emitter fills it in once and every consumer reads the same properties in the
same places, whatever produced them. Three properties of the type do the real
work.

It is **versioned**, so a consumer can say which schema it understands and
refuse anything else. It is **hashed**, so a consumer can tell whether the
payload it is holding is the payload the emitter sealed. And it is
**provenance-tracked**, so an approximation cannot quietly lose the identity
of the thing it approximated.

```{r class}
params <- data.frame(a = c(0.12, 0.15), b = c(1.51, 1.44))

m <- orchestra_manifest(
  emitter_package    = "example",
  emitter_version    = "0.1.0",
  inferential_target = "parameters",
  run_id             = "example-001",
  method             = "example:demo",
  seed               = 7L,
  params             = params,
  timestamp          = as.POSIXct("2026-07-05 09:00:00", tz = "UTC"),
  data_hash          = manifest_data_hash(params, NULL, NULL, NULL, 7L)
)

m@emitter_package
m@manifest_version
```

The properties fall into four groups. Identity says what this is and what made
it. Semantics says what it is about, drawn from a closed vocabulary a consumer
can dispatch on before it inspects any payload.

```{r targets}
inferential_targets()
```

Every current member of the orchestra that emits a manifest declares one of
these eight labels, read from that member's own manifest source rather than
re-derived here.

```{r targets-table, echo = FALSE}
token_emitters <- data.frame(
  token = inferential_targets(),
  emitting_member = c(
    "PESTO, proxymix, optimix, apsimR",
    "gpfield, apsimR",
    "kernR",
    "decideR",
    "flexyBayes",
    "flexyBayes",
    "cdzoo",
    "quorum"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(
  token_emitters, col.names = c("Inferential target", "Emitting member(s)"),
  caption = paste0(
    "The closed target vocabulary and which orchestra member emits each, ",
    "current at the time of writing."
  )
)
```

Payload carries the load-bearing content -- `params`, `outputs`, `weights`,
`obs_target`, `summary` and `seed` -- and is exactly the set the hash covers.
Provenance records what the result was derived from.

The diagram below draws the promise as a flow, from an emitter building the
payload through to a consumer either receiving a typed manifest or being
refused.

```{r flow-diagram, echo = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.cap = "The emit-verify-consume flow. An emitter builds the hashed, versioned, provenance-tracked manifest; verify_manifest() recomputes the payload hash; consume_manifest() adds the version gate and either hands the consumer a typed manifest or refuses -- on a version it does not accept, or a payload whose hash no longer matches."}
nodes <- data.frame(
  label = c("Emitter\nbuilds payload + hash",
           "orchestra_manifest()\nversioned, hashed,\nprovenance-tracked",
           "verify_manifest()\nrecomputes\nthe hash",
           "consume_manifest()\nversion gate\n+ verify",
           "Consumer\nreads the\ntyped payload",
           "Refusal\nwrong version or\nmismatched hash"),
  x = c(1L, 3L, 5L, 7L, 9L, 9L),
  y = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1.7, 0.3),
  kind = c("build", "object", "check", "check", "accept", "refuse"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
edges <- data.frame(
  x = c(1.85, 3.85, 5.85, 7.75, 7.75),
  y = c(1, 1, 1, 1.2, 0.8),
  xend = c(2.15, 4.15, 6.15, 8.25, 8.25),
  yend = c(1, 1, 1, 1.6, 0.4),
  path = c("flow", "flow", "flow", "accept", "refuse"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_rect(
    data = nodes,
    ggplot2::aes(xmin = x - 0.9, xmax = x + 0.9, ymin = y - 0.38,
                ymax = y + 0.38, fill = kind)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(
    data = nodes, ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
    size = 2.9, lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(
    data = edges,
    ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend, linetype = path),
    arrow = ggplot2::arrow(length = ggplot2::unit(0.15, "cm"),
                           type = "closed"),
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "stage", guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(flow = "solid", accept = "solid", refuse = "dashed"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10.3), ylim = c(-0.2, 2.3)) +
  ggplot2::theme_void() +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "The manifest contract: emit, verify, consume")
```

```{r flow-diagram-skip, echo = FALSE, eval = !requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), results = "asis"}

    "skipped.\n")
```

## Do

### Emit, verify, consume

The hash is taken over the payload only. Schema version, emitter identity and
timestamp are metadata, so re-tagging a manifest leaves an unchanged payload
verifying, while any edit to the payload is caught.

```{r verify}
verify_manifest(m)$ok

m@emitter_package <- "relabelled"
verify_after_relabel <- verify_manifest(m)$ok
verify_after_relabel
```

Tampering with the payload is a different matter.

```{r tamper}
tampered <- m
tampered@params$a[1] <- 0.99

verify_tamper <- verify_manifest(tampered)
verify_tamper
```

`verify_manifest()` returns its verdict as data because a consumer often wants
to record a failure and carry on with the other lenses it has. The loud
version is `consume_manifest()`, which is what a gate should call. It runs
three checks -- is this a manifest, is its schema one I accept, does its
payload still verify -- and errors on any of them.

```{r consume, error = TRUE}
run_id_consumed <- consume_manifest(m)@run_id
run_id_consumed

consume_manifest(tampered)
```

The version check is the one that earns its keep. Coercing silently across a
schema boundary is how a pipeline ends up reading a slot that no longer means
what it meant when the consumer was written, and the failure surfaces far
downstream as a wrong number rather than as an error.

```{r version, error = TRUE}
consume_manifest(m, accept = "1.0.0")
```

### Provenance is not optional for a derived result

A manifest that approximates another one records a compact handle to it. The
handle carries the upstream `data_hash`, not just its `run_id`, so a later
re-emission that changed the numbers cannot be passed off as the same input.

```{r lineage}
lin_m <- manifest_lineage(m)
lin_m
```

Setting `metadata$derived` to `TRUE` turns the lineage from a convention into
a rule the class validator enforces.

```{r derived, error = TRUE}
orchestra_manifest(
  emitter_package    = "proxy",
  emitter_version    = "0.1.0",
  inferential_target = "parameters",
  run_id             = "proxy-001",
  method             = "proxy:demo",
  metadata           = list(derived = TRUE),
  timestamp          = Sys.time(),
  data_hash          = manifest_data_hash(data.frame(), NULL, NULL, NULL,
                                          NA_integer_)
)
```

### A verdict is not an ensemble

A causal test or a decision produces one labelled conclusion, not a matrix of
draws. Forcing it into `params` as a single-row table leaves a consumer unable
to tell a verdict from a degenerate posterior, so it gets a typed home of its
own in `summary`. Because `summary` is inside the hash, a tampered verdict is
detected exactly like a tampered payload.

```{r summary}
verdict <- manifest_summary(
  "insufficient evidence",
  abstained = TRUE,
  abstain_reason = "effective sample size below the floor",
  metrics = list(ess = 41)
)

verdict$abstained
verdict$abstain_reason
```

### Refusals and abstentions

An abstention is a result, not a failure. A component that will not stand
behind a number should say so in a way a gate can recognise, and the problem
is that recognition used to depend on knowing which component produced it.
More than one component exports a predicate named `is_refusal()`, each
recognises only its own class, and when two are attached the bare name
resolves to whichever was attached last -- returning `FALSE` on the other
component's genuine refusal. That is a silent false negative, and a gate that
should have stopped sails straight through it.

The contract fixes this with a naming convention plus a pair of
producer-agnostic predicates. A structured refusal has a class ending in
`_refusal` and a structured abstention a class ending in `_abstention`, which
holds across object systems because the class vector of an S3 refusal and of
an S7 one both end that way.

```{r refusal}
s3_refusal <- structure(list(why = "no data"), class = "example_refusal")
s7_refusal <- structure(list(),
                        class = c("example::example_refusal", "S7_object"))
abstention <- structure(list(), class = "example_abstention")

refusal_flags <- c(is_orchestra_refusal(s3_refusal),
                   is_orchestra_refusal(s7_refusal))
refusal_flags
```

Gate logic almost always wants the wider union, because a refusal and an
abstention mean the same thing to a gate.

```{r decline}
decline_flags <- vapply(list(s3_refusal, s7_refusal, abstention, 42),
                        is_orchestra_decline, logical(1))
decline_flags
```

Seam-side code that mints a refusal of its own has no component name to follow
the convention with, so it stamps the explicit marker instead. The stamp is
idempotent, and a refusal can therefore pass through several layers without
accumulating duplicate classes.

```{r marker}
refusal_marker <- as_orchestra_refusal(structure(list(why = "capital firewall"),
                                                 class = "list"))
class(refusal_marker)
identical(as_orchestra_refusal(refusal_marker), refusal_marker)
```

### Grounding tokens

The grounding vocabulary is orthogonal to the refusal contract: a token says
how well a fact is evidenced, a refusal says what happened to the control
flow. A fact is grounded only when its verification date is present.

```{r tokens}
g_full <- grounding_token(as.Date(c("2026-07-05", "2026-07-06")))
g_partial <- grounding_token(as.Date(c("2026-07-05", NA)))
g_empty <- grounding_token(as.Date(character(0)))
g_full
g_partial
g_empty
```

The asymmetry is the point. An empty evidence set is not neutral, it is the
absence of evidence, and a partially checked set is not partially trustworthy
because the consumer cannot tell which element it may lean on. Both collapse
to `` `[unverified]` `` so a downstream gate errs towards abstention. Combining
tokens follows the same rule, worst-case across the inputs.

```{r combine}
c_both_grounded <- combine_grounding(c(GROUNDING_GROUNDED, GROUNDING_GROUNDED))
c_mixed <- combine_grounding(c(GROUNDING_GROUNDED, GROUNDING_UNVERIFIED))
c_both_grounded
c_mixed
```

Any other rule -- a majority, a mean, an optimistic "at least one" -- would
let a verdict inherit confidence from its checked inputs while quietly resting
on an unchecked one.

### Comparing two manifests on meaning, not position

A purely structural conformance check cannot catch a wrong-but-agreed
convention. Two components that both label a column `o1` will compare happily
even when one means tonnes per hectare and the other kilograms per hectare,
and the resulting number is wrong by a factor nobody downstream can recover.

The guard compares the semantic descriptors rather than the column positions,
and refuses on a disagreement.

```{r schema, error = TRUE}
with_unit <- function(unit, run_id) {
  orchestra_manifest(
    emitter_package    = "example",
    emitter_version    = "0.1.0",
    inferential_target = "predictions",
    run_id             = run_id,
    method             = "example:demo",
    obs_schema = list(outputs = data.frame(name = c("o1", "o2"),
                                           quantity = "grain_yield",
                                           unit = c(unit, "t/ha"))),
    timestamp          = Sys.time(),
    data_hash = manifest_data_hash(data.frame(), NULL, NULL, NULL,
                                   NA_integer_)
  )
}

assert_obs_schema_correspondence(with_unit("t/ha", "a"),
                                 with_unit("t/ha", "b"))

assert_obs_schema_correspondence(with_unit("t/ha", "a"),
                                 with_unit("kg/ha", "b"))
```

The check is opt-in by presence: when either manifest lacks an `obs_schema` it
is a graceful no-op, so the guard activates once both emitters populate the
field and no existing pipeline breaks on the day it lands.

### Adapting a component

A component joins the contract by being adapted, not by being rewritten. It
keeps its own result type and a method on `as_orchestra_manifest()` lifts that
type into a manifest. Two adapters ship here, for a `PESTO` ensemble manifest
and a `proxymix` mixture fit, and each is registered at load time only when
its component is installed.

```{r adapter, echo = requireNamespace("proxymix", quietly = TRUE), eval = requireNamespace("proxymix", quietly = TRUE)}
set.seed(1)
draws <- matrix(stats::rnorm(200), 100, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("a", "b")))
fit <- proxymix::fit_proxymix(proxymix::gmm_target_from_samples(draws),
                              N = 2L, regime = "sample", max_iter = 50L)

proxy <- manifest_from_gmm(fit, seed = 1L, consumed = list(m))

proxy@emitter_package
proxy@metadata$derived
proxy@consumed_manifests[[1]]$run_id
verify_manifest(proxy)$ok
```

```{r adapter-skip, echo = FALSE, eval = !requireNamespace("proxymix", quietly = TRUE), results = "asis"}
cat("proxymix is not installed on this build, so the adapter",
    "demonstration is not run here.\n")
```

### Two class identities, one contract

The contract was a script sourced into a coordination workspace before it was
a package. A manifest minted by that reference carries the bare class name,
one minted here carries the package-qualified name, and a component that
implements the contract without depending on this package mints the bare form
too.

```{r identity}
class(m)
is_orchestra_manifest(m)
```

They are the same contract, so identity is tested on the class name -- the
part the contract actually fixes -- rather than with a strict class check that
would reject every manifest emitted anywhere else.

```{r read-prep, echo = FALSE}
consume_tamper_msg <- tryCatch(consume_manifest(tampered),
                               error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
version_refusal_msg <- tryCatch(consume_manifest(m, accept = "1.0.0"),
                                error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
derived_refusal_msg <- tryCatch(orchestra_manifest(
  emitter_package    = "proxy",
  emitter_version    = "0.1.0",
  inferential_target = "parameters",
  run_id             = "proxy-001",
  method             = "proxy:demo",
  metadata           = list(derived = TRUE),
  timestamp          = Sys.time(),
  data_hash          = manifest_data_hash(data.frame(), NULL, NULL, NULL,
                                          NA_integer_)
), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
read_n_targets <- length(inferential_targets())
has_proxymix <- requireNamespace("proxymix", quietly = TRUE)
```

## Read

The opening question was what a manifest promises and how a broken promise is
caught. `inferential_targets()` names `r read_n_targets` closed labels --
including `consensus`, the label this release adds -- so a consumer can
decide whether it understands a manifest before it inspects any payload. The
identity properties (`emitter_package`, `manifest_version`) sit outside that
promise: relabelling `m@emitter_package` after the manifest was built leaves
`verify_manifest(m)$ok` at `r verify_after_relabel`, because metadata moved
and the payload did not. Editing `params$a[1]` by one hundredth instead flips
it to `r verify_tamper$ok`, reported as `r verify_tamper$message`.

`consume_manifest()` layers the version gate on top of that same check.
Calling it on the tampered manifest refuses with `r consume_tamper_msg`;
asking it to accept a version this build does not emit refuses with
`r version_refusal_msg`. Both are errors a caller cannot silently step past,
which is the point -- a manifest either verifies under an accepted schema or
the pipeline stops there, loudly, rather than three functions later on a
wrong number nobody can trace back to its source. The provenance rule refuses
the same way at construction: a manifest declaring `metadata$derived = TRUE`
with no `consumed_manifests` refuses with `r derived_refusal_msg`, so an
approximation cannot be minted without a traceable handle to what it
approximated.

The refusal and abstention predicates close the same gap from the producer's
side. `is_orchestra_refusal()` recognises the S3 and the S7 refusal alike
(`r paste(refusal_flags, collapse = ", ")`), and the wider
`is_orchestra_decline()` recognises all three declines but not the bare
integer sitting among them (`r paste(decline_flags, collapse = ", ")`) -- a
gate written against the union cannot be fooled by which object system
produced the decline. Grounding tokens collapse the same direction: a
partially dated evidence set and an empty one both read `r g_partial` and
`r g_empty`, and combining a grounded token with an unverified one keeps the
pair at `r c_mixed` -- the worst case of the two, never an average. The
verdict built above carries its own reason rather than a bare flag:
`abstained` is `TRUE` because `r verdict$abstain_reason`.

```{r read-text, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
if (has_proxymix) {
  cat(
    "The proxymix adapter carries the same promise across a package",
    "boundary: compressing the class chunk's manifest through",
    "`fit_proxymix()` and `manifest_from_gmm()` returns an",
    "`orchestra_manifest` whose `emitter_package` reads",
    paste0("\"", proxy@emitter_package, "\", whose `metadata$derived` is"),
    paste0(proxy@metadata$derived, ", whose"),
    "`consumed_manifests[[1]]$run_id` still names",
    paste0("\"", proxy@consumed_manifests[[1]]$run_id,
           "\", the manifest it compressed, and whose own hash verifies"),
    paste0("(", verify_manifest(proxy)$ok, ").\n")
  )
} else {
  cat(
    "proxymix is not installed on this build, so the adapter",
    "demonstration above did not run and its claims are unexercised",
    "here.\n"
  )
}
```

## Limits

The token-to-emitter table above is read from each member's own manifest
source at the time of writing -- the `inferential_target = "..."` literal in
its own `R/manifest.R` or equivalent, cross-checked against the constellation
roster -- not exercised by a call into that package from here. A member that
changed its target without a compatible version bump would leave the table
stale until this vignette is refreshed. Only two adapters are demonstrated
end to end, for PESTO and proxymix, because those are the two this package
ships; the other six members named in the table implement the contract
independently inside their own packages, each with its own worked example,
and are not re-run here.

Every manifest built in this vignette carries a two-parameter toy payload or
a hundred-draw mixture fit, small enough to keep the render fast rather than
to represent a production-scale ensemble or a spatial field. The
cross-implementation oracle that actually grounds the claim that "the same
contract" means bit-identical rather than merely similarly shaped -- building
a manifest under this package and under the reference implementation in
separate R sessions and requiring the two digests to match -- lives in the
package's test suite, not in this vignette.

## What to read next

*The Ensemble-Run Manifest: a Portable, Verifiable Record* walks PESTO's own
emission of the manifest this vignette wraps, from the calibration-ensemble
side. *Compressing a Bayesian posterior you can evaluate but not sample* is
proxymix's account of the same adapter from its side, including the
compression this vignette only calls once. *A quorum of lenses on Study A0*
and *Adding a lens* are quorum's two vignettes, the newest emitter of the
`consensus` target this release adds. *A benchmark harness and recommender
for causal discovery* is cdzoo's account of the `structure` target.

## Reproduce

Every result in this vignette is a deterministic function of the toy payload
built in the class chunk above, except the proxymix adapter demonstration,
which draws its hundred-observation mixture sample under `set.seed(1)`.
Package versions follow.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
